stem: In a survey of 100 professionals, each reads at least one of three journals P, Q, and R. Given n(P) = 45, n(Q) = 38, n(R) = 42, n(P intersect Q) = 12, n(Q intersect R) = 15, and n(P intersect R) = 10, find n(P intersect Q intersect R), the number who read all three journals.

per_option_rationale.rationale: By inclusion-exclusion: 100 = 45+38+42 - 12-15-10 + n(PQR) = 88 + n(PQR), so n(PQR) = 12.
This comes from computing 125 - 37 - 100 + 17 = 5, using an incorrect intermediate step that mis-sums the pairwise intersections as 32 rather than 37.
This comes from ignoring that n(union) = 100 and instead solving min(pairwise intersections) - 10 = 2, treating the problem as a minimum-overlap puzzle instead of back-solving the formula.
This comes from taking n(PQ) + n(QR) + n(PR) - n(U)/5 = 37 - 29 = 8, confusing the formula by subtracting a fraction of n(U) rather than using the full inclusion-exclusion identity.

explanation: Three-set inclusion-exclusion: n(P union Q union R) = n(P)+n(Q)+n(R) - n(PQ) - n(QR) - n(PR) + n(PQR). Since every professional reads at least one journal, n(union) = 100. Substituting: 100 = (45+38+42) - (12+15+10) + n(PQR) = 125 - 37 + n(PQR) = 88 + n(PQR). Therefore n(PQR) = 12.

explanation_sections.punchline: Back-solve the three-set inclusion-exclusion formula by using n(union) = 100 to isolate the triple intersection.
explanation_sections.approach: State the three-set formula: n(A union B union C) = sum of singles - sum of pairs + triple. Plug in all known values and solve for the triple intersection. The key setup move is recognising that at-least-one means n(union) = n(U) = 100.
explanation_sections.lesson: Three-set inclusion-exclusion alternates signs: +singles, -pairs, +triple. Back-solving from n(union) is the standard exam move.
explanation_sections.timing: 90 s. The hidden move is identifying n(union) = n(U) = 100, which is buried in the phrase each reads at least one.
